Arthur Ashe. An American tennis pioneer and civil rights advocate who won three Grand Slam singles titles and broke the color barrier in professional tennis. Beyond his on-court achievements, his intelligence, grace, and activism made him one of sports's most influential and respected figures in the twentieth century. He won the Australian Open in 1970, the US Open in 1968, and Wimbledon in 1975. He was the first African American man to win the US Open in 1968 and also to win Wimbledon in 1975, breaking through in an era when racial barriers in tennis were still significant and deeply entrenched. Known for his intelligent, all-court game, his versatility and tactical awareness set him apart from power-based contemporaries who relied more on pure strength. He became a major figure in the civil rights movement and later a fierce advocate for AIDS awareness after contracting HIV from a blood transfusion in 1983. This made him one of the first major athletes to publicly address the disease. He reached world number one in 1975 and won the Australian Open title at age thirty-five, one of the oldest first-time majors winners in the sport's history. He died in 1993, and his legacy extends far beyond tennis into humanitarianism, education, and social justice.
